title: A study of misinformation in whatsapp groups with a focus on the brazilian presidential elections
screen_reason: Observational study of 130 public Brazilian political WhatsApp groups during the 2018 presidential election. 50,795 URLs were extracted and 38,800 were coded with the Oxford 'junk news' grounded typology; junk news sources account for 13.1% of all coded links, with platform-specific shares for links pointing to YouTube (30.9%) and Facebook (42.3%). These are shares of SHARED links classified unreliable, i.e. SHARING (content_share) estimates with stated denominators.

estimates.date: 21 September - 20 October 2018 (the paper's table notes say 'Sept 21 to Oct 10, 2018')
estimates.measure_type: % of all coded links shared in Brazilian political WhatsApp groups that pointed to junk news sources
estimates.value_raw: Junk News 5,093 links = 13.1% of 38,800 coded links
estimates.denominator: 38,800 successfully labelled links (86.1% of the 45,072 analysed), extracted from 50,795 URLs shared in 130 public Brazilian political WhatsApp groups (5,723 whatsapp.com group-invite links were removed first)
estimates.definition: Link resolved to a source classified 'Junk News and Information': sources that 'deliberately publish misleading, deceptive or incorrect information purporting to be real news about politics, economics or culture', meeting at least three of five criteria (professionalism, style, credibility, bias, counterfeit)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Junk News and Information. These sources deliberately publish misleading, deceptive or incorrect information purporting to be real news about politics, economics or culture. This content includes various forms of propaganda and ideologically extreme, hyper-partisan or conspiratorial news and information.'
estimates.source_quote: sources account for 13.1% of all links in our dataset (see Table 1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: A team of coders applied a previously developed grounded typology (Howard et al., refined on Twitter and Facebook links across multiple elections) at the domain/sub-domain level, requiring at least 3 of 5 criteria for the junk-news label; Facebook pages were labelled at page level and YouTube at channel level. Inter-coder reliability Krippendorff's alpha = 0.84. Only YouTube and Facebook links shared five or more times were individually labelled.
estimates.moderator_quote: We accessed the chat history from 130 public groups and extracted 50,795 URLs shared within these groups. Out of these 5,723 URLs pointed to the whatsapp.com domain itself. ... We analyzed the remaining 45,072 links and successfully labeled 38,800 links, achieving 86.1% coverage of the dataset.
estimates.notes: SHARING (content_share), not CONTENT: the denominator is links that were SHARED in the groups, which the instructions assign to SHARING ('% of shared links unreliable' is SHARING). breadth is blank because the classification is source-level (a domain typology), not a claim-by-claim veracity judgement. ground_truth=researcher_coding because the authors' own coders applied the typology to domains; an adjudicator could equally read the resulting source classification as domain_list. denom_scope=political_news because the frame is groups 'dedicated to discussion of politics, news and current affairs', although the link set also contains non-political material (Video/Image sharing 16.8%, lifestyle etc.), so all_media is a defensible alternative. CAVEATS: 13.9% of analysed links could not be labelled and are excluded from the denominator; YouTube and Facebook links shared fewer than 5 times were never coded (the authors argue the coded set is representative by volume but not by variety); and snowball recruitment from public invite repositories may bias towards politically aligned groups, as the authors themselves note. DATE DISCREPANCY: the text says collection ran 21 September - 20 October 2018 while the source line under Tables 1 and 2 says 21 September - 10 October 2018.  QUOTE NOTE: the v2 text extraction interleaves the article's columns, so no longer contiguous span of the published sentence is recoverable; source_quote is the exact contiguous span carrying the value, and the full published sentence is: "Looking specifically at links being shared within WhatsApp groups, we note that junk news sources account for 13.1% of all links in our dataset (see Table 1)." (Findings, p. 1015); Table 1 row: "Junk News 5,093 13.1".

Platform stays WhatsApp because that is where the sharing was observed; YouTube is the destination. Only 494 of 1,549 Facebook links (32%) were coded because of the 5-share threshold, so this is the most heavily truncated cell in the paper and the 42.3% is likely an upper bound; confidence medium for that reason. missed_or_uncertain: (1) The third row of Table 2, 'Other news and Information Sources' (25,822 links shared, 19,549 coded, 1,407 junk = 7.2%), is the remaining destination subset and was not given a row: it is the complement of the two the paper headlines, and three subset rows plus the pooled row would multiply double-counting risk. The value is recorded here verbatim for an adjudicator who wants it. (2) IMAGE AND VIDEO SAMPLES: Tables 3 and 4 classify a random sample of 200 videos and 200 images (21-28 September 2018) into content categories crossed with political orientation. The 'Polarizing / Junk Content' row would give 36/200 = 18% of videos and 38/200 = 19% of images, but reaching those totals requires SUMMING the four political-orientation columns, which R8 forbids as a cross-category sum, and the paper never prints a total or a percentage ('the number of Polarizing and Junk images and videos is high'). The cell counts do reconcile exactly to 200 in both tables, so an adjudicator may judge the sums admissible. Related categories in the same tables that are NOT misinformation per se: Hate, Gore and Porn (19 videos, 7 images), Satire (31 videos, 42 images). (3) 'Reports have indicated that out of the top 50 most widely diffused images, 46 were fake or distorted' is attributed to a news report (Epoca, ref 10) and is excluded by R8 as a figure the paper cites from elsewhere. (4) 'Media files (99,988) accounted for 33% of all messages collected (298,892)' is a message-composition figure, not a misinformation share. (5) NO CONCENTRATION row is possible: the paper reports no top-X%-of-users/sources to Y%-of-sharing pair, so R1 fails. (6) No exposure, reach or survey measure exists in this paper.

rob.design: Observational digital-trace study of 130 public Brazilian political WhatsApp groups, joined via public invite links found through Google/DuckDuckGo and group repositories (gruposwhats.com, gruposdozapzap.com.br, linksdegruposzap.com) using Portuguese political keywords, then snowballed via invites circulating inside those groups. Collection 21 September - 20 October 2018 (table note says 10 October): 298,892 messages and 99,988 media files; 50,795 URLs extracted, 5,723 whatsapp.com invite links removed, 45,072 analysed, 38,800 labelled (86.1% coverage). Coding: a pre-existing grounded typology of news-source types with a 5-criteria junk-news definition (at least 3 of 5 required), applied at domain/sub-domain level, and at page/channel level for Facebook and YouTube; only Facebook and YouTube links shared 5+ times were individually coded. Inter-coder reliability Krippendorff's alpha = 0.84. Image/video sub-study: random sample of 200 videos and 200 images (21-28 September), coded to an exploratory typology with no reliability statistic reported. Authors' stated limitations: snowball sampling does not represent all public groups, group size and membership turnover are high, and initial-seed bias may cluster politically aligned groups. Ethics: Oxford CUREC approval, consent message posted on joining, data pseudonymised, no personal messages used.
